title: Nest Building
paragraphs: Another week of rain went by, and then the high blue arch of the sky came back, and the sun poured down hot and bright. Mistress Mary had not been able to visit either the secret garden or Dickon, but she had enjoyed herself very much anyway. The week had not felt long. Every day she spent hours with Colin in his room, talking about Rajahs, or gardens, or Dickon and the cottage on the moor. They looked through his splendid books and pictures. Sometimes Mary read aloud to Colin, and sometimes he read a little to her. When he was amused and interested, she thought he hardly looked like an invalid at all. Only his colorless face and the way he was always on the sofa gave it away.

“You were a sly one, listening in the night and climbing out of bed to go hunting for whatever was crying,” Mrs. Medlock said once. “But I can’t say it hasn’t turned out to be a blessing for all of us. He hasn’t had a single tantrum or whining fit since you two became friends. The nurse was ready to give up the case because she was so sick of him, but she says she doesn’t mind staying now that you’ve joined her on duty,” and she laughed a little.

While she talked with Colin, Mary tried hard to be careful about the secret garden. There were things she wanted to find out from him, but she felt she had to learn them without asking direct questions. First, now that she was beginning to like being with him, she wanted to know whether he was the kind of boy who could keep a secret. He was nothing like Dickon, but he was so delighted by the idea of a garden that nobody knew about that she thought he might be trusted. Still, she hadn’t known him long enough to be sure. The second thing she wanted to learn was this. If he could be trusted—if he truly could—might it be possible to take him to the garden without anyone finding out? The grand doctor had said Colin needed fresh air, and Colin had said he wouldn’t mind fresh air in a secret garden. Perhaps if he had plenty of fresh air, and met Dickon and the robin, and saw things growing, he would stop thinking so much about dying. Lately Mary had caught sight of herself in the mirror and realized she looked like a very different creature from the child who had arrived from India. This child looked nicer. Even Martha had noticed the change.

“The air from the moor has done you good already,” Martha had said. “You’re not nearly so yellow, and not nearly so scrawny. Even your hair doesn’t lie flat and slimy on your head. It’s got some life in it now, so it sticks out a bit.”
“It’s like me,” said Mary. “It’s growing stronger and fatter. I’m sure there’s more of it.”
“It looks that way, for sure,” said Martha, ruffling it up around her face. “You’re not half so ugly when it’s like that, and with a bit of red in your cheeks.”
If gardens and fresh air had been good for Mary, perhaps they would be good for Colin too. But then, if he hated people looking at him, maybe he wouldn’t want to see Dickon.
“Why does it make you angry when people look at you?” she asked one day.

“I’ve always hated it,” he answered, “even when I was very little. Then they took me to the seaside, and I would lie in my carriage, and everyone would stare. Ladies would stop and talk to my nurse, and then they would start whispering, and I knew they were saying I wouldn’t live to grow up. Sometimes the ladies would pat my cheeks and say ‘Poor child!’ Once, when a lady did that, I screamed out loud and bit her hand. She was so frightened that she ran away.”
“She thought you had gone mad, like a dog,” said Mary, not sounding admiring at all.
“I don’t care what she thought,” said Colin, frowning.
“I wonder why you didn’t scream and bite me when I came into your room,” said Mary. Then she slowly began to smile.
“I thought you were a ghost or a dream,” he said. “You can’t bite a ghost or a dream, and if you scream at them, they don’t care.”
“Would you hate it if—if a boy looked at you?” Mary asked, not sure how he would take it.
He lay back on his cushion and thought for a moment.
“There’s one boy,” he said very slowly, as if he were weighing every word, “there’s one boy I don’t think I would mind. It’s the boy who knows where the foxes live—Dickon.”
“I’m sure you wouldn’t mind him,” said Mary.
“The birds don’t mind him, and neither do other animals,” he said, still thinking it over. “Maybe that’s why I wouldn’t. He’s a sort of animal charmer, and I’m a boy animal.”
Then he laughed, and she laughed too. In fact they ended up laughing a great deal, because the idea of a boy animal hiding in his hole struck them as very funny indeed.
Afterward, what Mary felt was that she didn’t need to worry about Dickon.

On the first morning that the sky was blue again, Mary woke very early. The sun was pouring in through the blinds in slanting rays, and it looked so joyful that she jumped out of bed and ran to the window. She pulled up the blinds and opened the window itself, and a great wave of fresh, sweet-smelling air blew in on her. The moor was blue, and the whole world looked as if something Magic had happened to it. Tender little fluting sounds came from here and there and everywhere, as if dozens of birds were beginning to tune up for a concert. Mary put her hand out of the window and held it in the sun.
“It’s warm—so warm!” she said. “It will coax the green points to push up and up and up. The bulbs and roots under the ground will work and struggle with all their might.”

She knelt and leaned as far out of the window as she could, breathing deep and sniffing the air. She sniffed until she began to laugh, remembering how Dickon’s mother had said the tip of his nose quivered like a rabbit’s.
“It has to be very early,” she said. “The little clouds are all pink, and the sky has never looked like this before. Nobody is awake. I can’t even hear the stable boys moving about.”
A sudden thought made her scramble to her feet.
“I can’t wait! I’m going to see the garden!”

By now she had learned to dress herself, and she was ready in five minutes. She knew of a small side door that she could unbolt on her own. She flew downstairs in her stocking feet and put her shoes on in the hall. She took off the chain, drew the bolts and turned the lock. When the door was open, she sprang over the step in one bound, and there she stood on the grass, which seemed to have turned green. The sun poured down on her, sweet warm breezes drifted around her, and fluting and twittering and singing came from every bush and tree. She clasped her hands for pure joy and looked up at the sky. It was so blue and pink and pearly and white, and so flooded with springtime light, that she felt she had to flute and sing aloud herself. She knew that thrushes and robins and skylarks could not possibly help it either. She ran around the shrubs and along the paths toward the secret garden.

“It’s all different already,” she said. “The grass is greener, and things are sticking up everywhere. Things are uncurling, and green buds of leaves are showing. I’m sure Dickon will come this afternoon.”

The long warm rain had done strange things to the flower beds that bordered the walk by the lower wall. Shoots were sprouting and pushing out from the roots of the plant clumps. Here and there, among the stems of the crocuses, there were even glimpses of royal purple and yellow unfurling. Six months earlier, Mistress Mary would not have noticed how the world was waking up, but now she missed nothing.

She reached the place where the door hid itself under the ivy, and a strange loud sound startled her. It was the caw—caw of a crow. It came from the top of the wall, and when she looked up, there sat a big, glossy blue-black bird, looking down at her very wisely indeed. She had never seen a crow so close before, and he made her a little nervous. But in the next moment he spread his wings and flapped away across the garden. She hoped he wasn’t going to stay inside, and she pushed the door open, wondering if he would. When she had gone well into the garden, she saw that he probably did mean to stay. He had landed on a dwarf apple tree, and under the apple tree lay a little reddish animal with a Bushy tail. Both of them were watching the stooping body and rust-red head of Dickon, who was kneeling on the grass, working hard.
Mary flew across the grass to him.
“Oh, Dickon! Dickon!” she cried out. “How did you get here so early! How could you! The sun has only just come up!”
He got to his feet, laughing and glowing and tousled, his eyes like a bit of the sky.

“Eh!” he said. “I was up long before him. How could I have stayed in bed! The world’s all begun again this morning, it has. It’s working and humming and scratching and piping and nest-building and breathing out scents, till you’ve got to be out in it instead of lying on your back. When the sun jumped up, the moor went mad for joy. I was right in the middle of the heather, and I ran like mad myself, shouting and singing. And I came straight here. I couldn’t have stayed away. Why, the garden was lying here, waiting!”
Mary put her hands on her chest and panted, as if she had been running herself.
“Oh, Dickon! Dickon!” she said. “I’m so happy I can hardly breathe!”

Seeing him talking to a stranger, the little bushy-tailed animal got up from its place under the tree and came to him. The rook cawed once, flew down from its branch and settled quietly on his shoulder.

“This is the little fox cub,” he said, rubbing the little reddish animal’s head. “His name’s Captain. And this here’s Soot. Soot flew across the moor with me, and Captain ran as if the hounds were after him. They both felt just the same as I did.”
Neither creature looked the least bit afraid of Mary. When Dickon began to walk around, Soot stayed on his shoulder, and Captain trotted quietly close to his side.
“Look here!” said Dickon. “See how these have pushed up, and these, and these! And Eh! Look at these here!”

He threw himself down on his knees, and Mary dropped beside him. They had come upon a whole clump of crocuses that had burst into purple and orange and gold. Mary bent her face down and kissed them again and again.
“You never kiss a person like that,” she said when she lifted her head. “Flowers are so different.”
He looked puzzled, but he smiled.
“Eh!” he said. “I’ve kissed Mother that way many a time, when I come in from the moor after a day of roaming, and she’s standing at the door in the sun, looking so glad and comfortable.”

They ran from one part of the garden to another and found so many wonders that they had to remind themselves to whisper or speak low. He showed her swelling leaf buds on rose branches that had looked dead. He showed her ten thousand new green points pushing up through the soil. They put their eager young noses close to the earth and sniffed its warm springtime breath. They dug and pulled and laughed low with delight, until Mistress Mary’s hair was as tumbled as Dickon’s and her cheeks were almost as poppy-red as his.

There was every joy on earth in the secret garden that morning. In the midst of them came a delight more delightful than all the rest, because it was more wonderful. Something swiftly flew across the wall and darted through the trees to a thickly grown corner. It was a little flare of a red-breasted bird with something hanging from its beak. Dickon stood quite still and put his hand on Mary, almost as if they had suddenly found themselves laughing in a church.

“We mustn’t stir,” he whispered in broad Yorkshire. “We mustn’t hardly breathe. I knew he was hunting for a mate when I saw him last. It’s Ben Weatherstaff’s robin. He’s building his nest. He’ll stay here if we don’t frighten him.”
They settled down softly on the grass and sat there without moving.

“We mustn’t seem to be watching him too close,” said Dickon. “He’d be cross with us for good if he got the notion we were interfering now. He’ll be a good bit different till all this is over. He’s setting up housekeeping. He’ll be shyer and quicker to take things badly. He’s got no time for visiting and gossiping. We must keep still a bit and try to look like grass and trees and bushes. Then, when he’s got used to seeing us, I’ll chirp a bit, and he’ll know we won’t be in his way.”

Mistress Mary was not at all sure she knew how to look like grass and trees and bushes, the way Dickon seemed to. But he had said the odd thing as if it were the simplest and most natural thing in the world. She felt it must be quite easy for him. In fact, she watched him carefully for a few minutes, wondering whether he could quietly turn green and put out branches and leaves. But he only sat wonderfully still. When he spoke, he dropped his voice so softly that it was strange she could hear him, but she could.

“It’s part of the springtime, this nest-building is,” he said. “I’d wager it’s gone on the same way every year since the world began. They’ve got their own way of thinking and doing things, and a body had better not meddle. You can lose a friend in springtime easier than in any other season, if you’re too curious.”
“If we talk about him, I can’t help looking at him,” Mary said, as softly as she could. “We must talk about something else. There’s something I want to tell you.”
“He’ll like it better if we talk of something else,” said Dickon. “What is it you’ve got to tell me?”
“Well—do you know about Colin?” she whispered.
He turned his head to look at her.
“What do you know about him?” he asked.
“I’ve seen him. I’ve gone to talk with him every day this week. He wants me to visit. He says I’m helping him forget he’s ill and dying,” answered Mary.
As soon as the surprise faded from his round face, Dickon looked truly relieved.
“I’m glad of that,” he exclaimed. “I’m right down glad. It makes me easier. I knew I mustn’t say anything about him, and I don’t like having to hide things.”
“Don’t you like hiding the garden?” said Mary.

“I’ll never tell about it,” he answered. “But I said to Mother, ‘Mother,’ I said, ‘I’ve got a secret to keep. It’s not a bad one, you know that. It’s no worse than hiding where a bird’s nest is. You don’t mind it, do you?’”
Mary always wanted to hear about his mother.
“What did she say?” she asked, not at all afraid to hear.
Dickon grinned good-naturedly.
“It was just like her, what she said,” he answered. “She gave my head a bit of a rub and laughed, and she said, ‘Eh, lad, you can have all the secrets you like. I’ve known you twelve years.’”
“How did you know about Colin?” asked Mary.

“Everybody who knew about Mr. Craven knew there was a little lad who was likely to be a cripple, and they knew Mr. Craven didn’t like him talked about. Folks are sorry for Mr. Craven because Mrs. Craven was such a pretty young lady and they were so fond of each other. Mrs. Medlock stops at our cottage whenever she goes to Thwaite, and she doesn’t mind talking to Mother in front of us children, because she knows we’ve been brought up to be trustworthy. How did you find out about him? Martha was in fine trouble the last time she came home. She said you’d heard him fretting and you were asking questions, and she didn’t know what to say.”

Mary told him her story. She told about the wind wuthering at midnight, which had woken her, and the faint, far-off sounds of the complaining voice, which had led her down the dark corridors with her candle. She told how it had ended with her opening the door of the dimly lit room, with the carved four-posted bed in the corner. When she described the small ivory-white face and the strange black-rimmed eyes, Dickon shook his head.

“They’re just like his mother’s eyes, only hers were always laughing, so they say,” he said. “They say Mr. Craven can’t bear to look at him when he’s awake. It’s because his eyes are so like his mother’s, and yet they look so different in his miserable little face.”
“Do you think he wants to die?” Mary whispered.

“No, but he wishes he’d never been born. Mother says that’s the worst thing on earth for a child. Those who aren’t wanted hardly ever thrive. Mr. Craven would buy anything money could buy for the poor lad, but he’d like to forget he’s even alive. For one thing, he’s afraid he’ll look at him some day and find he’s grown a hunchback.”
“Colin is so afraid of it himself that he won’t sit up,” said Mary. “He says he’s always thinking that if he felt a lump coming, he’d go crazy and scream himself to death.”
“Eh! He shouldn’t lie there thinking things like that,” said Dickon. “No lad could get well while he thinks that sort of thing.”

The fox was lying on the grass close beside him, looking up now and then to ask for a pat. Dickon bent down and rubbed its neck gently, and he thought for a few minutes in silence. Then he lifted his head and looked around the garden.
“When we first got in here,” he said, “everything seemed gray. Look around now and tell me if you don’t see a difference.”
Mary looked, and her breath caught a little.
“Why!” she cried. “The gray wall is changing. It’s as if a green mist were creeping over it. It’s almost like a green gauze veil.”
“Aye,” said Dickon. “And it’ll get greener and greener until the gray is all gone. Can you guess what I was thinking?”
“I know it was something nice,” said Mary eagerly. “I think it was something about Colin.”

“I was thinking that if he was out here, he wouldn’t be watching for lumps to grow on his back. He’d be watching for buds to break on the rose-bushes, and he’d likely be healthier,” Dickon explained. “I was wondering if we could ever get him in the mood to come out here and lie under the trees in his carriage.”

“I’ve been wondering about that too. It crosses my mind almost every time I talk with him,” said Mary. “Could he keep a secret? Could we bring him here without anyone seeing? I thought maybe you could push his carriage. The doctor ordered fresh air for him, so if he asks us to take him outside, nobody will dare say no. He won’t go out with other people, and they may even be glad if he goes with us. He could tell the gardeners to stay away, and then they’d never find out.”
Dickon was thinking very hard as he scratched Captain’s back.

“It’d be good for him, I’ll warrant,” he said. “We’d not be thinking he’d be better off never born. We’d be just two children watching a garden grow, and he’d be another. Two lads and a little lass just looking on at the springtime. I warrant it’d be better than doctor’s medicine.”

“He’s spent so long lying in his room, always terrified about his back, that it’s made him odd,” said Mary. “He’s learned plenty from books, but nothing else. He says he’s been too sick to notice anything around him. He hates going outside, and he hates gardens and gardeners. Still, he likes hearing about this garden, because it’s a secret. I didn’t dare tell him much, but he told me he wanted to see it.”

“We’ll have him out here sometime, for sure,” said Dickon. “I could push his carriage well enough. Have you noticed how the robin and his mate have been working while we’ve been sitting here? Look at him perched on that branch, wondering where it’d be best to put the twig in his beak.”

He whistled one of his low calls. The robin turned his head and gave him a questioning look, his twig still in his beak. Dickon talked to him much as Ben Weatherstaff did, but his tone was friendly advice.
“Wherever you put it,” he said, “it’ll be all right. You knew how to build your nest before you came out of the egg. Get on with it, lad. You’ve got no time to lose.”

“Oh, I do like to hear you talk to him!” Mary said, laughing with delight. “Ben Weatherstaff scolds him and teases him, and he hops about and looks as if he understands every word, and I know he likes it. Ben Weatherstaff says he’s so conceited that he’d rather have stones thrown at him than not be noticed.”
Dickon laughed too and kept on talking.
“You know we won’t trouble you,” he said to the robin. “We’re nearly wild things ourselves. We’re building a nest too, bless you. Mind you don’t tell on us.”

The robin did not answer, because his beak was full. But when he flew off with his twig to his own corner of the garden, Mary knew that the darkness of his dew-bright eye meant he would not tell their secret for the world.
